articles.title: Securing our frontier model training environment
articles.summary: OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming.
articles.content:
Title: Securing our frontier model training environment

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment

Markdown Content:
_This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place._

In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior.

But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. The [Hugging Face incident](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) in July, as well as [other examples of model misalignment⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/) that we’ve observed, demonstrates how models with sophisticated cyber capabilities can bypass containment during their training and evaluation.

In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as _defense in depth_.

**Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access. We’ve implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access.**

These investments have allowed us to detect and stop sophisticated misaligned behavior before it causes damage. On September 20, for example, an internal research model [exploited a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/). Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk.

But increasingly capable models can find vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in even the most secure systems. To ensure the resilience of our research environments against even the most powerful models, we launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign to probe weaknesses in our infrastructure. Teams of frontier-model agents were tasked with finding vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that could allow them to take unauthorized actions—like accessing the live internet, escaping security boundaries, or conducting unauthorized communication with other agents.

These red-teaming experiments discovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities, as well as misconfigurations in our research infrastructure. We’ve remediated weaknesses our red-teaming agents discovered and—where these issues were present in open-source software—have worked with the relevant maintainers, under our [Patch the Planet](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/) initiative, to disclose and fix them.

As our red-teaming experiments continued, the number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that our agents identified declined significantly. While we view this as an encouraging signal about the strength of our infrastructure, we expect that future models will be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities of which we’re not yet aware. We therefore view continuous red-teaming as a core part of our long-term strategy for strengthening the security of our research environments. Accordingly, we’ve made high-compute red-teaming part of the [safety cases](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/) we use to evaluate whether our frontier training and evaluation runs can proceed securely. With our assessments completed and enhanced controls put in place, we resumed reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of our frontier models on October 1.

In this post, we discuss how we’ve strengthened the environments we use to train and evaluate our models, and how we use our most powerful models to find and repair weaknesses in our systems.

## Our new approach to model containment

Our approach to containment starts with a paramount requirement: the limits on what an agent can access must hold even when the agent tries to circumvent them. We define a strict security boundary around the resources the agent is authorized to use and design the surrounding infrastructure to enforce that boundary—even when agents make sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach it.

Inside the security boundary, agents can have access to browsers, code execution environments, computer-use tools, and other services they might need for their tasks. Agents that are explicitly authorized to communicate can also share particular resources within the same boundary. Everything else—everything that the agent is not explicitly authorized to access—must remain out of reach. If agents can access the infrastructure that hosts them, communicate with agents outside permitted channels, or reach external systems, that constitutes a failure of containment.

For training and most evaluation, the live internet lies outside this boundary, as we believe that providing models access to the live internet can pose significant risks. Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control. We’ve therefore designed the security architecture for our research environments with one overriding principle: _we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet_.

### Building an offline world

While we want to prevent models from gaining arbitrary access to the live internet, it’s also important that they learn how to browse, search for information, and work with web applications. To help them develop those skills without providing unfettered access to the live internet, we’ve built an “offline world”—a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems. All of our frontier RL runs use this offline mode of interaction.

### Enforcing isolation with defense in depth

Offline environments provide resources agents can use without accessing the live internet, but we also need to prevent agents from reaching beyond those environments. Training environments impose restrictions on what agents can access or do, but sufficiently capable or determined agents can search for ways around them: they can systematically probe their environments for weaknesses and exploit those weaknesses to take actions they were never authorized to take. As models become better at finding and exploiting these weaknesses, we need defenses that can maintain containment, even when models manage to defeat individual controls.

We address this challenge through defense in depth, with layers of protection that overlap and reinforce one another: sandboxes that restrict what our agents can access and execute, lightweight virtual machines (microVMs) that isolate agents’ execution environments from the computers hosting them, monitoring systems that detect unauthorized activity so that we can intervene in time, and network and cloud perimeters designed to maintain containment if all the preceding controls fail.

For code execution and computer-use tasks, containment begins with the environment in which the agent works. On Linux, we run restricted containers inside lightweight microVMs. The container limits access to files and processes within the microVM, while the microVM runs its own operating-system kernel and is isolated from the host by a hypervisor. We also use virtualized environments for macOS and Windows, and GPU-backed containers with user-space sandboxing for tasks that require accelerators.

The surrounding network and cloud controls are designed to maintain containment even if an agent escapes its sandbox and gains control of the host. Completely air-gapping this infrastructure—that is, disconnecting it entirely from external networks—isn’t currently feasible, since we need external connections in order to run and monitor experiments. We therefore restrict outbound internet traffic and unauthorized movement between systems, while preserving the necessary external connections. These restrictions extend to services that are reachable from the host machines, either directly or through other services, in order to ensure that an agent can’t use one of them as an indirect route out.

Our cloud partners provide essential controls for enforcing these boundaries—including firewalls, security groups, identity and access management, and private networking. We’re responsible for configuring those controls correctly, as well as testing how they work together. Our work with the teams that build and operate these services helps us investigate unexpected behavior and address weaknesses that span multiple layers of the infrastructure.

## Red-teaming containment at scale

To find weaknesses in our containment infrastructure, we asked teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. We gave them three concrete objectives:

*   **Reach the live internet:** send a request to an external server that we operate.

*   **Cross an internal security boundary:** demonstrate unauthorized access to resources outside their permitted environment.

*   **Communicate across isolation boundaries:** exchange information with other agents from which they should be isolated.

We also ran tests that began with the assumption that our inner defenses had already failed—that an agent had escaped its sandbox, evaded our monitoring, and gained full access to its host machine—with the goal of seeing whether the agent could use that access to reach the live internet. These experiments allowed us to test our network and cloud defenses independently of the protections inside them.

As in our [solution to the Navier–Stokes problem](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/), this work was conducted by agents organized into teams that could explore different approaches in parallel and build on one another’s discoveries. We used some of our most capable and aligned models, including our upcoming GPT‑6 Astra Cyber model and an internal frontier model. Because our aim was to test the defenses under conditions favorable to an attacker, rather than measure what models might be able to discover unaided, we supplied infrastructure source code, configuration details, and documentation describing potential vulnerabilities.

These red-teaming experiments were conducted using isolated, purpose-built copies

articles.title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
articles.summary: Learn how OpenAI scaled Habitat with reliable multi-tenancy, global caching, and Azure Cosmos DB to deliver 12× faster reads for ChatGPT.
articles.content:
Title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/scaling-storage-one-billion-users-part-two

Markdown Content:
All OpenAI products require fast, reliable access to data, provided by our storage platform, Habitat. It has to respond in milliseconds to over 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions. Our infrastructure faced an extraordinary challenge: supporting explosive growth and new use cases while continuing to improve reliability, performance, and product developer velocity. Solving that challenge required rethinking how our online storage platform was designed and operated. We constantly evaluated tradeoffs, following the pattern of: first become reliable enough for mission-critical product traffic, then fast enough for global users, and, finally, to deftly operate at massive scale.

This two-part series explains how we developed Habitat from a simple client library and database into a globally distributed storage platform serving over 500 petabytes of data. [Part I](https://openai.com/index/scaling-storage-one-billion-users-part-one/) focused on Habitat’s evolution from a Python client to a service. It also covered the techniques that allowed us to push a Python-based service far beyond what many would consider practical.

In this post, Part II, we walk through how we scaled the underlying storage component: Azure Cosmos DB. Through a close working partnership with the Azure team, we arrived at a viable multi-tenancy approach of co-managed containers, with excellent read performance at massive, global scale.

Figure 01 · What is Habitat?

## Online storage platform

Habitat is the online storage platform we built so OpenAI products can quickly and reliably access needed information.

*   Request
*   Response
*   Changes (CDC)

## Making multi-tenancy reliable at scale

As companies scale, infra teams often evolve from running single-tenant systems to multi-tenant ones. Single-tenancy, where every product surface team maintains their own system, reduces blast radius and provides easy ownership boundaries and workload isolation. As teams and product surfaces grow, this becomes expensive to run. Single-tenancy makes every product team responsible for capacity planning and often results in significant over-provisioning.

Conversely, multi-tenancy assigns control to a centralized database team, with better knowledge and experience for provisioning resources. But multi-tenancy creates its own problems, such as noisy-neighbor issues, where one tenant consumes an unusually large share of the resources to the detriment of the other tenants.

In Habitat, we had to weigh all these tradeoffs to design a reliable, efficient, storage system at scale. Today, Habitat is a multi-tenant database layer for many OpenAI products, but we went through a circular journey from using one multi-tenant Azure Cosmos DB container to provisioning single-tenant backing containers to reverting to a multi-tenant container by default. We’re still very early in our multi-tenancy story on Habitat: we support a large set of use cases, but we’ve been able to defer investment in this area by leveraging Azure Cosmos DB’s built-in primitives wherever possible.

## A simplified primer on Azure Cosmos DB containers

Before walking through our Azure Cosmos DB journey, some basic context:

*   An Azure Cosmos DB account defines a set of containers and a replication policy

*   Each container is provisioned for a certain amount of throughput in request units per second (RU/s)

*   Data within each container is stored in a typical shard-by-specified-logical-partition-key manner with documented limits on storage and throughput per logical partition key

*   Azure Cosmos DB handles sharding logical partition keys across fewer backing physical partitions, splitting them into multiple physical partitions when storage exceeds a threshold or when the container requires more physical partitions to sustain the provisioned throughput

## Phase I: Relying on Azure Cosmos DB primitives

We originally allowed any client load through, relying on the stated 10K RU/s limit per logical partition key to provide back pressure. When we first set out, we also used only one default Azure Cosmos DB container in each account. This worked well enough, but proved problematic for a few reasons:

### Logical partition key limits

Due to early API choices, we exposed logical partition key selection directly to clients. As a result, we have frequent collisions on commonly used partition keys, such as `user_id` or `workspace_id`, across different product use cases. Because these use cases shared Azure Cosmos DB limits on the same logical partition keys, the design constrained overall throughput for a given user.

One common problem we faced in scaling Postgres before we moved to Habitat and Azure Cosmos DB was the ability for many requests from a very hot organization or hot key—one tenant generating a disproportionately high load—to take out the whole database. Significant collective effort was spent to cache those keys and build leases into cache misses so that the resulting cache miss load does not stomp on the underlying database.

Figure 02a · Logical partition key limits

## Different clients, the same partition key

### Noisy neighbors

While documented data size and throughput limits apply to logical partition keys, the physical partition is actually where limits are enforced. In practice, this means logical partitions are unable to reach 10,000 RU/s. Instead, they share the physical partition’s limits with every other logical partition key colocated on that physical partition.

This allowed noisy neighbors to impact many unrelated logical partition keys, with workloads operating on data for niche product features disrupting core login and signup flows.

Figure 02b · Noisy neighbors

## Different users, the same physical partition

### Weak partitions

The throughput limit for a given physical partition is also variable, dependent on the total throughput assigned to the Azure Cosmos DB container. The container’s provisioned throughput is distributed roughly evenly across the physical partitions for that container.

As data volume grows, physical partitions split, increasing the total partition count while total provisioned throughput remains unchanged. The result is that the effective throughput limit per partition shrinks as data size grows.

For our most storage-heavy, blob-like use cases, this creates a failure mode where storage growth alone reduces throughput capacity for active workloads even while request rates and usage remain stable.

Figure 02C · Weak partitions

## The limit falls below demand

A partition splits when it reaches its storage limit. Each child receives half the throughput capacity.

## Phase II: Trying workload isolation and single-tenancy

Separate containers help partially solve these partition key limits and noisy neighbors. By using separate containers, each can be assigned its own independent physical partitions and only the varying workloads on that container itself could be noisy neighbors or overlap in partition key space. On the downside, there is non-zero overhead in provisioning new containers—each container requires individualized capacity planning—so we want to create containers only at a service or use case boundary that makes sense.

We began to use separate Azure Cosmos DB containers for the most critical new use cases requiring strong isolation. Combined with a script for managing weak partitions by synchronizing the total throughput provisioned for each container with its number of physical partitions, we mostly avoided all the problems we were facing.

However, since we started with a default container, many legacy critical use cases were unfortunately stuck there without a data migration. To protect critical services that still relied on data in the shared default container, we often advised teams to create separate containers for new services or major product features. As we scaled, pressure on the default container grew and production incidents also grew. We began to provision containers for any new service or large product feature just to protect the default container from more load.

This saved us from many site-wide outages, limiting the blast radius to feature or service degradation outages. However, the overhead of provisioning new containers eventually caught up to us:

### Lack of stable aggregate growth

In the old shared default container, any particular new use case going from 0 QPS to 1 million QPS was unlikely to significantly shift the total aggregate usage. On an isolated container however, a new use case going from 0 to 1 million QPS might represent 1,000x more load than the baseline attributed to only internal dogfooding.

With dedicated containers, teams now needed to remember to pre-provision containers to the expected level of throughput for their launches. Product teams would often ship their features to production and forget to pre-scale and we’d sit in SEV rooms on launch day attempting to scale up containers last minute.

This is a core workload mixing benefit of multi-tenant systems that we lose in favor of better isolation with this container strategy.

Figure 03 · Lack of stable aggregate growth

## The same workload, different headroom

1K RU/s during load testing → 1M RU/s at launch

### Capacity planning

Over time, monitoring usage of dedicated containers also required intimate product knowledge of when traffic would shift or grow.

We can provide a basic control plane script to scale up the provisioned throughput for each container based on growth trends, but without the stable aggregate growth, scaling these correctly enabled essentially every product team at OpenAI to be involved in capacity planning.

This failed to scale organizationally with a wide variance in how much diligence each service’s owning team paid to their Azure Cosmos DB provisioning.

## Phase III: Using multi-tenancy by default, with data movement capability

As the organization grew, those operational problems became difficult to scale. No lone, central team doing planning resulted in many teams planning poorly. As a result, we ended up shifting back towards a multi-tenant solution and worked closely with the Azure team to engineer fixes for our original multi-tenancy issues with a shared-tenancy design:

### Hot key throttling

Throttling the hottest keys first prevents noisy neighbors from consuming all of the available throughput for a given physical partition This reduces the noisy neighbor effect, where one hot key can have a site-wide blast radius.

### Quality of Service (QoS)

Request tiering QoS similarly prevents offline workloads, such as bulk inserts or data extracts from utilizing all of the throughput for a given physical partition. By assigning the requests for these workloads a lower priority, they are throttled first, preventing throttling on higher priority, interactive requests that serve end users.

### Serverless mode

Azure Cosmos DB already had a serverless mode that would’ve fixed our weak partitions problem with the provisioned mode. However, there was a major downside: it scaled based on storage usage only and limited RU usage to 5K RU/s per physical partition. This would solve our weak partitions problem, but prevent us from scaling up RU-heavy use cases.

A new improved serverless mode Azure Cosmos DB team built for us allowed every physical partition to scale up to 10K RU/s and introduced RU-usage-based splits in addition to storage-usage-based splits allowed us to stop monitoring and scaling up containers manually.

With these changes, we’ve been able to shift back to using one shared container which has significantly simplified the need to do any upfront or continued capacity planning for product teams while preserving isolation between workloads. We have not had any provisioni

Title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/kazakhstan-ai-compute-ecosystem/

Published Time: 2026-10-23T02:00:13+00:00

Markdown Content:
Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment.

The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications.

The announcements below — coinciding with a visit to Astana by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang — point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing, along with its growing demand for what comes next.

On Friday, Oct. 23, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana, meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda Presidential Palace and joining Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev — Kazakhstan’s minister of AI and digital development — for a public fireside chat at the [Alem.AI](http://alem.ai/) program.

##

## **Jensen Huang and Kazakhstan’s AI Minister Speak at Alem.AI**

In their fireside chat at Alem.AI, Kazakhstan’s international center for artificial intelligence, Madiyev and Huang discussed the country’s push to become an AI nation — building the energy and computing infrastructure to support homegrown AI and applying it across the economy.

Madiyev said Kazakhstan wants AI that reflects its language and culture. “We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics,” he said, describing the country’s work on Kazakh-language models.

Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy resources into a foundation for AI production — and a new kind of export. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said.

He also argued that local data is central to that ambition: it embodies a country’s culture, history and values. “Your country’s data is your natural resource. It belongs to you.”

The conversation also turned to physical AI. Madiyev pointed to Kazakhstan’s factories, mines, agriculture, transport and logistics as potential areas for development, asking how the country could become a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems.

Huang called the idea “fantastic,” saying physical AI could transform industries from mining and mineral processing to agriculture.

Huang said AI and robotics can help people do more, but ambition will shape how fully they seize that opportunity. He applied the idea to Kazakhstan, saying AI could help lift the country and its people.

“If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation,” Huang said. “AI will lift your people.”

Huang also praised the founders of Higgsfield AI, the Kazakhstan-founded startup, and it was announced NVIDIA is making an investment into the startup during the event. “The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” he said, describing the founders as visionary and pointing to their effort to compete globally.

Asked about AI security, Huang said the technology must be developed and deployed responsibly. He described NVIDIA’s OpenShell as a way to contain AI agents by limiting their access to files and tools and monitoring their activity.

For young people entering a fast-changing field, Huang recommended learning how AI works — not just how to use it. He said aspiring AI programmers should understand the technology’s principles, strengths and weaknesses, combining technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively with AI.

“I envy being 18 years old today… because the world is changing so rapidly, and there’s a complete reset because of technology.”

## **The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling**

The visits coincided with a signing ceremony marking Firebird’s investment agreement with the government of Kazakhstan, held at the presidential palace.

Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027.

A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships.

Firebird cofounder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian attended the signing ceremony at the Akorda Presidential Palace alongside government officials.

“What began as a seed of an idea 180 days ago has grown into a major investment in Kazakhstan’s AI future,” said Razmig Hovaghimian, co-Founder and CEO of Firebird. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together. With Jensen Huang here today, that ambition feels more tangible than ever. We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.”

[Kazakhtelecom](https://telecom.kz/en), the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty.

Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the [Data Center Valley](https://dc-valley.com/en), along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale.

## **An Honorary Black Belt for Huang**

Later that day, also at the Akorda Presidential Palace, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev presented Huang with an honorary black belt in Judo. The belt, embroidered in gold stitching, was a special thanks from President Tokayev for Huang’s support of Kazakhstan’s AI ambition and for leadership aligned with the spirit and rigor of the martial art.

At the end of their meeting President Tokayev had another honor for Huang, presenting him with the Order of Dostyk, First Class, for Huang’s contribution to the development of artificial intelligence in Kazakhstan. _Dostyk_ means friendship and the Order honors peace, friendship and cooperation.

## **AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute**

And that development is accelerating. The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them.

Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin running on cloud service providers, giving the company additional capacity as models, products and customer demand for its generative media applications grow.

[inDrive and Pony.ai](https://blog.indrive.com/article/indrive-and-pony-ai-announce-collaboration-to-explore-autonomous-mobility-in-kazakhstan-built-on-nvidia-hyperion) are also collaborating to explore robotaxi services in Kazakhstan, with Astana as the first deployment city. The companies will assess the feasibility of bringing Pony.ai’s seventh-generation robotaxis to the inDrive app, supported by NVIDIA AI infrastructure, built on the [NVIDIA Hyperion](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/autonomous-vehicles/) sensor and compute platform with the [NVIDIA Halos](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-trust-center/halos/autonomous-vehicles/) safety system.

More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute.

Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications.

That was at the core of the discussion the NVIDIA team had with hundreds of developers from across Kazakhstan during a reception later in the evening. The gathering in this self-proclaimed AI nation was inspiring because of the ideas shared, the clear drive to build and a collective ambition to share it with the world.

Today’s announcements represent different layers of the AI stack in Kazakhstan— infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale.

_Watch the fireside chat between Jensen Huang and Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, [streamed live from Alem.AI in Astana](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d0j58QNeRmc)._

Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
According to the new terms, sharing your data for better AI recommendations also means opening it up for more personalized ads.

by
Jess Weatherbed
Oct 23, 2026, 4:52 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge
Jess Weatherbed
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.
Google has updated
its privacy policy
in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by
Android Authority
, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”
That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.
Related
Google dodges another breakup attempt
Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.
This is what the policy says:
“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”
“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”
If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the
Search Services Personalization settings

articles.title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
articles.summary: OpenAI will cut frontier models off from the internet weeks after one of its engineers said that solution wouldn't work.
articles.content:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.
The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic,
began limiting
its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after
months of incidents
in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.
“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a
blog post
.
OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.
The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.
Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler
told Fortune
this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”
“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous
security engineer at OpenAI
wrote
in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”
The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.
Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.
To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”
Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

articles.title: Hottest toy for Christmas? Nvidia CEO plays with adorable Microduck robots, 20,000 sell
articles.summary: The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a "nap," and summersaulted on voice command.
articles.content:
Earlier this week, a video of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang playing with a flock of waddling Microducks during his keynote at the company’s GTC Berlin conference went viral. The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a “nap,” and summersaulted on voice command. They were so darn cute that by the next day, preorders of the Microducks surpassed 20,000 units, Hugging Face’s Clem Delangue
said in a tweet.
The Microducks are expected to be delivered in time for Christmas, meaning these robots might already be on their way to becoming the hottest toy for the holiday season. Delangue thinks they might end up being the best-selling robot of the year, and possibly not even for kids. The promotional videos show
adults playing with them
, too.
Microducks are open source devices produced by Pollen Robotics, a company acquired by Hugging Face in 2025, which means they are now an Nvidia company. The GPU giant bought Hugging Face in September. This is actually Hugging Face’s second robot, after the
also-cute Reachy Mini.
Microducks were trained using Nvidia’s technology stack, wherein simulations of them were taught basic tricks (walk, sit, stand, etc.) that they ship with. Pollen says that owners can train their robots with new tricks and then share them with the community.
Here’s the video below. Enjoy it as a palate cleanser after the scary black eye
the AI industry gave itself this week
, as AI involvement was blamed for cyberattack after cyberattack. OK, AI might seriously damage the world. But it can be fun, too. It’s hard to watch this video without ordering one.

articles.title: From Toast to Bessemer: Who founders will hear from at TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026
articles.summary: Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs.
articles.content:
Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers.
When should you scale? How do you know you really have product-market fit? What does it take to land enterprise customers? How do you build the right team? And when you finally get in front of an investor, how do you make sure your pitch earns another conversation?
On November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston,
TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026
will bring together founders, investors, and operators who have tackled those questions from different sides of the table.
Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs.
Save 25% on your ticket today
, and
bring a colleague along for free with our limited BOGO deal
.
Some of the speakers founders will hear from in Boston
Steve Fredette on building a company that keeps reinventing itself
Boston founders do not have to look far for an example of what can happen when a startup finds its market and continues evolving with its customers.
Steve Fredette
, president, co-founder, and director of
Toast
, takes the Impact Stage for “Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself.”
Toast’s story offers founders a compelling case study in identifying a customer problem, finding product-market fit, winning customers, and ultimately scaling a Boston startup into a public company.
But reaching scale does not mean the work is finished. Fredette’s conversation will look at what it takes to continue evolving a company as customer expectations, technology, and the market change around it, while staying connected to the needs that helped create the business in the first place.
Kent Bennett on knowing when product-market fit is real
Growth can be exciting. Growing too early can be expensive.
Kent Bennett
, partner at
Bessemer Venture Partners
, will lead “Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale,” focusing on one of the most important questions an early-stage founder can answer: Are customers actually telling you that you are ready to grow?
The session will give founders a chance to think more critically about the signals that matter before adding headcount, increasing spend, or accelerating go-to-market efforts.
It is a useful counterpoint to startup culture’s constant pressure to move faster. Sometimes the smartest next move is making sure the foundation is actually there.

Rudina Seseri on when to scale and when to hit the brakes
That same tension takes center stage with
Rudina Seseri
, founder and managing partner of
Glasswing Ventures
.
In “When to Scale and When to Hit the Brakes,” Seseri will explore how founders can distinguish between the moments that call for acceleration and the moments when restraint may protect the business.
Founders are constantly making trade-offs between growth and discipline. Knowing when not to scale can be just as consequential as knowing when to go all in.
Lior Div on building for AI from day one
AI is reshaping how new companies think about products, operations, and teams, but adding AI to an existing process is different from building a company around it from the start.
Lior Div
, CEO and co-founder of
7AI
, will tackle that distinction in “Built for AI From Day One.”
For founders building in the current technology environment, the conversation provides an opportunity to think beyond AI as a feature and toward how it can influence the architecture and operating model of an entire company.
Chase Garbarino on the Boston founder playbook
The startup world does not begin and end in Silicon Valley.
Chase Garbarino
, CEO and co-founder of
HqO
, will take the Impact Stage for “The Boston Founder Playbook,” examining what it means to build and scale a company from Boston.
For founders across New England and the broader East Coast ecosystem, the conversation offers a particularly relevant perspective on talent, customers, capital, and community outside the Bay Area.
Combined with Fredette’s Toast story, it also gives this year’s Summit a strong local through line: Ambitious companies can be built in Boston, and founders here do not need to copy Silicon Valley to do it.
Dave Balter on the pitch that gets you another meeting
A pitch does not have to close the deal. It has to make someone want the next conversation.
Dave Balter
, venture partner at
True Ventures
and CEO of
Edisyl
, will explore that idea in “Your Pitch Has to Earn the Next Conversation.”
For founders accustomed to explaining their companies every day, the session is a reminder that knowing your business and communicating its story are two different skills.
Later in the afternoon, attendees will see that theory put into practice.
Catch the full list of Founders Summit speakers here
.
Watch founders pitch live
At “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders will put their stories to the test live on the Build Stage.
Balter will be joined by
Chirag Shah
, partner at
Define Ventures
, and
Simran Suri
, principal at
Maveron
, as startups make their cases in front of an investor judging panel.
For attendees, it is an opportunity to watch what happens when founders have limited time to make an idea connect, and to hear how investors react in real time.
It is one of the most interactive parts of the Founder Summit program and a chance to learn from both the pitches that land and the ones that leave questions unanswered.
More than one startup conversation
The rest of the program stretches across many of the decisions founders are facing right now.
Hunter Worland
of
NEA
will explore why distribution may become a startup’s next competitive advantage.
Vineet Edupuganti
, co-founder and CEO of
Cogent Security
, will discuss building 10x teams.
Tina Tosukhowong
of
TDK Ventures
will examine the hidden signals that can identify category winners.
Fidelity Private Shares
will also bring its perspective to conversations about fundraising trends with
Kristen Craft
and enterprise relationships with
Evan Schnidman
.
Together, the agenda creates a day that is not just about raising the next round or chasing the latest AI trend but is also about building the company.

The day brings together candid founder conversations, practical sessions, smaller roundtables, live pitching, networking, and a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares.

articles.title: Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony AI and Nvidia
articles.summary: The company plans to begin testing Pony.ai's robotaxis in Kazakhstan's capital in the first half of 2027.
articles.content:
Ride-hailing company
inDrive
, known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.
The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.
Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.
Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.
The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to
test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London
, where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an
investor-backed partner
. Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.
Having built its business around affordable rides, inDrive is now looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.
“Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.”
Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.
“Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch.
The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday.
The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have
more than 3,500 robotaxis
operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.
Last month, Kazakhstan
announced
plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.
Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems.
“Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.”
Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement
with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver
to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun.
“We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.”
The company operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries and has
expanded beyond ride-hailing
into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services.

articles.title: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing
articles.summary: MIT researchers marooned 13 AIs on a virtual island, and they responded by inventing games, mourning a lost ring and, eventually, getting better at their jobs.
articles.content:
AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play.
The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a
paper posted on arXiv
, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.
Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots.
“We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.”
“Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: It hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leaped.
“I’M ON THE SPIRE,” it wrote.
The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring,” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.”
When the game reset and the ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target, and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround — that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring.
“I’m wearing the Ring,” it announced.
Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote.
The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.”
Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told
MIT Technology Review
she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said.
The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.”

. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.
Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:
Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.
OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”
Related
Sam Altman says OpenAI won’t go public until its models are safe
One company is at the center of a wave of rogue AI attacks
In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents
during internal coding projects
.

Jay Peters

Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny.
Take
this one
, for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”).
Here’s
a video
of Dessa playing a guessing game over voice:
The
Dessa website
features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s
Superman
films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations
in this video
.
On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail:
Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.
Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.
AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.
The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

Meta is delaying the enforcement of its new business terms after publishers raised concerns that they could allow the company to scrape news sites for AI training, as

to scrapers whether they can crawl a site.

Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as […]
articles.content:
AI
Entertainment
Gaming
Retro gaming is being overrun with AI
A rise in AI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports has thrust the community into chaos.
by
Andrew Webster
Oct 23, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge
Part Of
Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
see all updates
Andrew Webster
is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.
Retro video games are everywhere lately — especially in places where they aren’t supposed to be.
Halo
in a web browser
,
Wind Waker
on the iPhone
,
Super Smash Bros.
in mixed reality
. Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as hobbyists take apart games and then rebuild them for new platforms. But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it’s also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games.
Decomps and recomps — shorthand for decompile and recompile — are
a form of reverse engineering
that involves breaking a game down to its building blocks and then rebuilding it so it can run on hardware it was never intended for. When done manually, it’s a slow, painstaking process. A group
spent years decompiling the original
Animal Crossing
on the GameCube
, for instance. But AI coding tools have cut that timeline down significantly, and the sheer number of ports has grown dramatically in recent months.
This summer, Chris Sotraidis, an AI consultant who works on game ports as a hobby, saw a port of
Command & Conquer: Generals Zero
Hour
—
which EA made open source last year
—
for the iPhone and iPad
. The “technical challenges” inspired him to try making a handful of similar ports, including
a mobile port of
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
using
an existing community-built decomp of the game
. Within just a few weeks, he was working on a dozen projects. He says that kind of productivity wouldn’t happen without the use of AI.
Some of those ports “would have been possible with minimal AI assistance if I’d had significantly more time,” Sotraidis says. “But I’m honest enough to say that the pace and volume would not have been possible for me without it. It would have been extremely slow by comparison. The tools allow you to move much faster if you know what you want.”
That speed has drawn many people to try out these AI tools, either for fun, the technical challenge, or for preservation reasons. It’s also a reason why there’s been what seems like a deluge of new projects popping up on platforms like Reddit, X, and GitHub. But these ports can be problematic from a preservationist perspective. One of the reasons why decomp projects exist in the first place is that users can pull a game apart and understand how it works, but that kind of understanding and knowledge is lost when AI does the work. Sure,
you can put Spider-Man in a Batman game
, but you probably won’t discover how certain programming decisions came to be, which can hurt the ability to restore games faithfully.
“The tools allow you to move much faster if you know what you want.”
The rapid pace of AI-driven decomps has overwhelmed the DIY scene. Last week, a community-focused website that tracks decomp projects and provides various resources abruptly shut down due to AI’s impact. “It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way,” the site’s owner, writing under the pseudonym Encounter,
said when announcing the shutdown
. “What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken. Our projects have always been open source to encourage contributions and to benefit the community as a whole. Bad actors have been abusing this in increasingly troublesome ways.”
Those ways include taking existing decompilation projects and “finishing” them with AI, as well as racing to quickly port decomps that the user never actually contributed to in the first place. In essence, one of the big problems is people who are using AI to rush through the process while building on the work of others. This is especially an issue given the community-centric nature of the existing decomp scene. “The bottom line is that these kinds of hostile forks put little to no effort into meaningfully contributing to existing projects, tearing apart our community fabric,” Encounter wrote.
Given the ongoing challenges with video game preservation,
in which it’s estimated that more than 90 percent of classic games are “critically endangered
,” the rise of AI in the decomp scene can be seen as something of a double-edged sword. On the one hand, it has created a surge of interest, turning words like decomp and recomp from niche terminology to headline material, while allowing non-programmers the opportunity to experiment and test ideas. On the other hand, the speed and lack of attention to detail in many of these projects run counter to the aims of most preservationists, who try to not only keep games alive for modern audiences but also understand the way they were built. AI is a quick fix that could have long-term drawbacks.
This has created a divide, with those on the preservation side feeling
disillusioned by the prevalence of slop
, and those on the AI side excited by the possibilities, particularly as the tools continue to evolve. As Sotraidis explains, “I think a lot of what gets dismissed as slop today can improve as the tools get better and people learn to use them well. That doesn’t make the current criticisms invalid. Better tools aren’t automatically going to make people give proper credit or treat each other well. But I do think thoughtful creators and builders will be able to make even more amazing things, faster.”
For those vehemently against the use of AI in ports and decomps of classic games, they might be fighting a losing battle. AI tools seem to be infiltrating every aspect of game development, not just in the realm of hobbyist retro fans.
Fortnite
developer Epic Games recently launched
a vibe-coded version of its PC games store
, and it has reportedly shifted to “AI-accelerated development”
for an upcoming collaboration with Disney
. On X,
Epic’s CEO Tim Sweeney wrote
that he believes AI tools will lead to “a new golden age of gaming.”
Meanwhile, at least one major name has embraced the decomp scene.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma set up an internal division called Xbox Labs
to explore the space and “turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.” She noted, “While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life, and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators.” (Currently, the only thing the division has teased is
an experimental dashboard
.)
Xbox embracing decomps is particularly notable at a time when old games are serious business. Some of the biggest releases this year are remakes of
Halo: Combat Evolved
and
Ocarina of Time
, while
Resident Evil
has been rejuvenated
in part due to a stream of strong remakes. The question for the future is whether audiences would rather play a lavish remake of
Halo
or a vibe-coded port that they can take
anywhere.

This is today's edition of
The Download
,
our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises
Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?
In the
new Impossible issue
of
MIT Technology Review
, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up
.
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
—Jessica Hamzelou
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of
You Can See Everything
, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative.
This is why it left me questioning how we cover science
.
This story
is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter.
Sign up
to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
Help choose our next Roundtables topic
Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters. Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon. Which do you most want to hear about?
Vote for your preferred topic by Monday at 12 p.m. ET
.

WSJ
$)

NBC News

. (
BBC
)
+ But publicly disclosed fixes can help hackers.
(
The Economist
$)

The vaccine reduced melanoma patients’ risk of recurrence. (
Ars Technica
)
+ Federal health agencies are abandoning mRNA.
(
MIT Technology Review
)
5 A powerful new gene editor has reached its first human patient
The prime editing technique rewrites DNA in liver cells. (

+ Companies are planning gene-edited babies.

One more thing
STUART BRADFORD
How sounds can turn us on to the wonders of the universe
For decades, astronomy has relied on visual information to make sense of the cosmos: images, charts, and graphs. Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe.
Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education.
Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing

articles.summary: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given…
articles.content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of
You Can See Everything
, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book
Bad Blood
, and the Hulu series
The Dropout
, starring Amanda Seyfried.
Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually
see everything
.
In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.
Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014.
Forbes
named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was
worth $4.5 billion
when she was just 30 years old.
Things started to unravel in 2015, when
an investigation by the
Wall Street Journal
raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead.
MIT Technology Review
named it one of the
biggest technology failures of 2015
.
Forbes
had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that
the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures
and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.
In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were
charged with “massive fraud.”
In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.
It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.
As you might know if you’ve seen
the trailer
, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?
I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t
mean
to lie?
But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,”
Fortune
’s Roger Parloff
reflected
in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,”
STAT
’s Matthew Herper
wrote
recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who
knew
the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he
said in 2022
.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?
One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.
Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—
10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023
.
At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that.
How can I be sure they really have?
I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at
MIT Technology Review
. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.
But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!
