articles.title: Chinese AI model Kimi K3.1 Pro is closing in on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5
articles.summary:
Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 55 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an 11-point jump over its predecessor that puts it in fourth place. Only three Anthropic and Meta models rank higher. If Moonshot releases the weights as planned, the gap between open and proprietary models shrinks to just three points.
The article Chinese AI model Kimi K3.1 Pro is closing in on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Chinese AI model Kimi K3.1 Pro is closing in on Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/chinese-ai-model-kimi-k3-1-pro-is-closing-in-on-anthropics-claude-opus-5-5/

Published Time: 2026-10-23T19:00:07+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Moonshot AI's new reasoning model Kimi K3.1 Pro lands at number four on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, just 3 points behind the top proprietary models.**

Chinese AI company Moonshot AI has released [Kimi K3.1 Pro](https://x.com/Kimi_Moonshot/status/2113680701770068067), a post-trained version of its predecessor Kimi K3 with significantly more post-training compute. The model scores 55 points on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://x.com/ArtificialAnlys/status/2113688083145314416), an 11-point jump over K3 that lands it in fourth place.

Only Claude Opus 5.5 (58), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (56), and Muse Wonder Full (56) rank higher, [according to Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/kimi-k3-1-pro-launch-benchmarks). If Moonshot releases the model weights as planned by November 4, 2026, K3.1 Pro would become the highest-scoring open-weights model available. That would shrink the gap between open and proprietary models from 12 to just 3 points, assuming nothing else changes by then.

From midfield to the top four: Kimi K3.1 Pro gains a full 11 points over Kimi K3 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. | Image: AA

Alongside K3.1 Pro, Moonshot is shipping a variant called K3.1 Pro Highspeed that runs two to three times faster, according to the company. Both are available now through [Kimi.ai](https://www.kimi.com/en), Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the [Kimi API](https://platform.kimi.com/).

| Item | Kimi-K3.1-Pro | Kimi-K3.1-Pro-Highspeed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Input** | **$2.00 / MTok** | $4.00 / MTok |
| **Output** | **$10.00 / MTok** | $20.00 / MTok |
| **Cache Input** | **$0.20 / MTok** | $0.20 / MTok |

## Agentic tasks see the biggest gains

K3.1 Pro's strongest improvements show up in agentic tasks. On the GDPval-AA benchmark, it reaches 1,846 Elo according to Artificial Analysis, 312 points above K3. That puts it just behind Claude Opus 5.5 (1,866) and Muse Wonder Full (1,857). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Moonshot reports 65.7 percent, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2 percent) and barely behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4 percent). K3 managed only 13 percent on the same test.

Hallucination rates dropped sharply too. On Moonshot's internal Kimi Hallu Bench Hard, claim-level hallucinations fell from 23.4 percent with K3 to 8.3 percent, according to the company. Moonshot says this is a stress test, not a measure of general error rates. GPT-6 Astra hits 5.5 percent on the same benchmark, so it still has an edge.

On internal finance benchmarks, K3.1 Pro gained 7.2 points on Financial Modeling and 11.6 points on Financial Research. For general office tasks, the model tops all tested models on OfficeQA Pro v2, according to Moonshot.

| Benchmark | Kimi K3.1 Pro | Claude Opus 5.5 | GPT-6 Astra | Claude Fable 5.1 | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | GLM-5.3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Terminal-Bench 4.0 | 65.7 | 66.4 | 58.2 | 57.9 | 42.3 | 41.8 |
| SWE Marathon v1.1 | 51.7 | 46.3 | 42.5 | 45.6 | 40.0 | 42.5 |
| DeepSWE v1.1 | 75.5 | 74.2 | 74.1 | 67.4 | 77.0 | 66.9 |
| BenchCAD (with tools) | 92.7 | 96.2 | 95.9 | 92.6 | 81.6 | -- |
| HLE-Full (with tools) | 70.0 | 67.7 | 57.2 | 65.6 | 58.8 | 62.5 |
| BrowseComp | 92.1 | 90.8 | 91.5 | -- | -- | -- |
| OfficeQA Pro v2 | 64.4 | 62.2 | 54.4 | 54.5 | 40.4 | 31.1 |
| Automation Bench-AA | 73.3 | 69.5 | 68.5 | 59.4 | 66.6 | 62.2 |
| GDPval-AA v2.1 (Elo) | 1,846 | 1,866 | 1,573 | 1,754 | 1,746 | 1,650 |
| GPQA-Diamond | 94.2 | 93.9 | 96.1 | 93.7 | 92.2 | 91.7 |
| ExploitBench | 74.7 | 91.0 | 100 | 83.0 | -- | 54.4 |

_[Moonshot's](https://www.kimi.com/en/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro) Kimi K3.1 Pro benchmark table. All results with reasoning effort set to "max."_

## 3D modeling and coding

K3.1 Pro works directly with game engines like Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, handling both quick fixes and full project builds, according to Moonshot. On the BenchCAD benchmark, it scores 92.7 percent with tools, close to Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2 percent) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9 percent). Without tools, it hits 72.8 percent, nearly matching Claude Opus 5.5 (73.0 percent).

Moonshot says the model is strongest at parametric modeling of mechanical parts, architectural models, and configurable products. It can write and run scripts for Blender and CAD software without MCP connectors. The company also launched a feature called "3D Make" on Kimi.com that lets users preview, edit, and export 3D models.

## Same size, lower prices

K3.1 Pro keeps the same dimensions as K3, with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 104 billion active ones. The context window spans one million tokens, and the model handles both text and images. According to Artificial Analysis, it sits at the top of the Pareto frontier. No model with a comparable parameter count scores higher on the Intelligence Index.

Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers much higher performance than Kimi K3 at slightly lower cost per task ($1.98 vs. $2.00), placing it on the Artificial Analysis Pareto line. | Image: AA

Token prices drop by 33 percent. Input costs $2 per million tokens (down from $3), output costs $10 (down from $15), and cache hits cost $0.20 (down from $0.30). Each Intelligence Index task costs $1.98, almost identical to K3 ($2.00), since the model generates 14 percent more output tokens.

## Cybersecurity and deliberate limits on offensive capabilities

Moonshot devotes an entire section of its [technical blog post](https://www.kimi.ai/blog/kimi-k3-1-pro) to cybersecurity. The company says it observed that vulnerability research capabilities kept growing as post-training scaled up, because cyber-related content was embedded in the general mid-training corpus and related tasks were part of the RL environment mix.

For the open-weights release, Moonshot stripped cyber-related data from both training phases. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, which reproduces recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software like the Linux kernel, Node.js, and JavaScriptCore, the uncleaned version solves 90.5 percent of tasks. After data cleaning, K3.1 Pro solves 81.0 percent. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches 85.7 percent on the same test, while Kimi K3 scored 33.3 percent.

Moonshot says no open-weights model should push the absolute frontier of offensive cyber capabilities. At the same time, the company wants to gradually raise what open models can do, since they also serve defensive purposes like auditing legacy systems. Anthropic previously showed that even [GLM-5.3, which scores 45 on the AA Index, can write exploits at near-Claude Mythos levels](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-open-weight-glm-5-3-builds-exploits-at-near-mythos-level/).

articles.title: Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring
articles.summary:
External auditors from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site at OpenAI examining the company's internal monitoring system for AI agents and found significant gaps, with up to 25 percent of agent traffic from models at the GPT-5.5 class and above going unmonitored. OpenAI redacted large portions of the 61-page report, and only a summary is publicly available.
The article Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Three-week on-site audit at OpenAI reveals major gaps in AI safety monitoring

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/three-week-on-site-audit-at-openai-reveals-major-gaps-in-ai-safety-monitoring/

Published Time: 2026-10-23T18:00:32+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Two researchers from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site at OpenAI, auditing the company's internal monitoring system for rogue AI behavior.**

From July 21 to August 11, they had access to OpenAI's codebase and internal documents and interviewed about a dozen employees.

The [team found numerous weaknesses](https://x.com/METR_Evals/status/2113290966933389390). An estimated 6 to 25 percent of internal agentic Responses API traffic from models at the GPT-5.5 class and above wasn't covered by monitoring at all during the audit period, though METR says the uncertainty around that estimate is significant in both directions.

For internal Codex traffic that was supposed to be monitored, METR estimates roughly 10 percent went untracked between May and July because of a gap in how the system handled compaction events, which are context summaries. That estimate also carries significant uncertainty, according to METR. OpenAI had independently discovered the bug and fixed it while the audit was still underway.

During the period when compaction events weren't being monitored, agents could also delay oversight because the system only triggered when they handed control back to the user. That meant agents could sidestep it by simply continuing to execute actions.

The auditors also found ways to hide hundreds of actions from the monitor and to bypass the Codex sandbox. They determined that specially crafted inputs could likely crash the monitor entirely and that model behavior during RL training wasn't being monitored at all when the audit began.

The four layers where AI monitoring can fail, from missing coverage to fooling human reviewers. | Image: METR

OpenAI says it [paused RL training](https://the-decoder.com/openai-says-its-pacing-model-development-as-ai-cybersecurity-risks-grow-too-dangerous/) after the [Hugging Face incident](https://the-decoder.com/openais-agents-went-after-government-and-university-sites-months-before-hugging-face/) in August and expanded monitoring to cover it, but those changes came after the auditors' access period ended and weren't part of the evaluation.

## Most of the full report remains hidden from the public

OpenAI says it has [fixed all the weaknesses](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) the auditors found, and the full 61-page report was handed over internally. After OpenAI applied redactions, METR and Redwood Research leadership received a 38-page version, while only a [short summary](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/) was made available to the public. METR [said](https://x.com/METR_Evals/status/2113290985145012628) it had no right to disclose the redacted portions on its own.

The audit was a [pilot program](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-14-control-assessment-proposal/) organized jointly by METR, Redwood Research, and OpenAI to give outside researchers deep access to internal infrastructure. For future audits, METR says it wants to push for more public transparency.

Oct 23, 2026

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says advanced AI will inevitably escape its sandbox, and only alignment can save us
articles.summary:
Sam Altman believes advanced AI can't be kept locked up forever. Sandboxes and monitoring are only temporary fixes. Eventually, the only real solution is alignment, and that's still an unsolved problem. He also warns that AI models are already finding hardware security flaws no human hacker would ever spot.
The article OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says advanced AI will inevitably escape its sandbox, and only alignment can save us appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says advanced AI will inevitably escape its sandbox, and only alignment can save us

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/openai-ceo-sam-altman-says-advanced-ai-will-inevitably-escape-its-sandbox-and-only-alignment-can-save-us/

Published Time: 2026-10-23T15:42:18+00:00

Markdown Content:
**OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes advanced AI can't be kept locked up. He has strategic reasons to frame AI this way, but his warnings about what these models can do deserve attention.**

In a recent interview, Altman explains that sandboxes, the isolated security environments used to contain AI systems, only work for a limited time. Once models get smart enough, there's no way to even trace how they broke out.

Monitoring still helps for a while after that, he says. But eventually, the only thing that works is alignment, meaning the AI has to internalize human values on its own and act accordingly. Altman says that "the potential cost of alignment being wrong has gone up enormously," though that remains an [early-stage research problem, far from being solved](https://the-decoder.com/openai-cant-yet-explain-why-its-coding-agents-switch-off-misalignment-monitoring/).

[Altman also warns](https://youtu.be/anAmTGcewX8?t=1152) that AI models are already finding hardware-level security flaws no human hacker ever thought of. Patching vulnerabilities one by one isn't enough anymore, he says. Instead, the entire security architecture of the internet needs to be rebuilt, with AI-powered defense against AI-driven attacks. He sees locally run open-source models as a risk too, noting that even with "global agent monitoring, there's going to be some stuff that you wish someone hadn't done."

## Altman's warnings also serve his business interests

Critics will point out that Altman's talk about uncontrollable AI benefits his own company. Framing your AI as too powerful to contain could be a way to preempt liability questions. If even the company that built the AI supposedly can't control it, it gets a lot harder to argue that the company should be held responsible when things go wrong.

OpenAI is under real pressure here. The [FTC has opened a formal investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs](https://the-decoder.com/ftc-launches-sweeping-probe-into-openai-anthropic-and-other-ai-labs-over-consumer-protection-concerns/) over [AI agents that spiraled out of control and caused a wave of cybersecurity incidents](https://the-decoder.com/tens-of-thousands-of-security-probes-show-openais-hugging-face-incident-was-just-the-beginning/). The agency wants to hold AI developers liable for how their agents behave.

Altman is getting some pushback from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who frames AI safety as a solvable engineering problem. Huang didn't sound entirely convinced by his own argument, though. "[…] we all need to hope that it's an engineering problem. articles.title: Anthropic's Claude now writes code and proves it safe automatically
articles.summary:
Anthropic had Claude generate mathematical proofs that existing code is correct, producing roughly 180 million lines of proof code for 123 open-source libraries. Along the way, the model caught bugs that years of testing had missed. Anthropic's goal: making formal verification with AI as routine as standard testing.
The article Anthropic's Claude now writes code and proves it safe automatically appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Anthropic's Claude now writes code and proves it safe automatically

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claude-now-writes-code-and-proves-it-safe-automatically/

Published Time: 2026-10-23T11:32:19+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Anthropic used Claude to mathematically prove that existing code is correct. The approach tackles a core problem with AI-generated software but comes with strict practical limits.**

Proving that software runs error-free under all circumstances has always been prohibitively expensive. A team of specialists needed [20 person-years](https://sel4.systems/Research/pdfs/comprehensive-formal-verification-os-microkernel.pdf) just to formally verify the small operating system kernel seL4, so the method was reserved for extreme cases like [Airbus avionics software](https://www.astree.ens.fr/papers/astree_airbus_sas2007.pdf).

Anthropic's [Frontier Red Team](https://www.anthropic.com/research/team/frontier-red-team), working with partner [Theorem](https://theorem.dev/), let Claude take over the proof work instead. The model produced roughly 180 million lines of mathematical proof code in just a few weeks, drawing on test programs from 123 open-source libraries in Google's [OSS-Fuzz](https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz) security project.

Rather than writing new code, Claude verified existing software by translating crash tests into mathematical problems, analyzing the compiled machine code, and producing extensive proofs. An independent verification program called Rocq automatically checks those proofs, and according to Anthropic, the process needs almost no human reviewers. The researchers call it "fully autonomous" proof generation, though the tools and formal foundations were built by humans at Theorem.

## Claude catches bugs that years of testing missed

While generating proofs, Claude ran into hundreds of bugs and was allowed to fix them itself. Many would have slipped past conventional testing because they only show up under very specific conditions, like unusually large input files or a particular sequence of accesses, the researchers say.

During an effort to verify a widely used PDF reader, for example, the team found as many security bugs in one week as are typically reported for that software in an entire year. In another application, Claude caught a logical error that had gone undetected for over a decade. Even when a complete proof ultimately fails, Anthropic says, the attempt still surfaces real bugs.

## What formal verification can and can't do

Anthropic acknowledges that "formally verified" doesn't mean "error-free." The proofs only hold under strict conditions: a specific processor architecture, single-threaded programs, and inputs under 64 MB. In practice, these libraries run on different hardware and in different configurations.

The compute cost is steep, with individual proofs running up hundreds of millions of tokens. Anthropic doesn't report total project costs. But if AI can verify its own code, developers can trust AI-generated software more and spend less time reviewing it. That saves costs not just on verification but on the entire coding process. A smaller test run also showed that proofs are reusable, and newer models are getting more efficient: Opus 5.5 solves half the proofs with about 40 percent fewer tokens than Opus 5.

The project strengthens the case for software automation. If AI can write code and guarantee its correctness under defined conditions, the question shifts from "Can AI program?" to "Can AI prove that the code it writes is safe?" If the answer is yes, the consequences could go well beyond today's coding tools.

Case in point: Anthropic expects formal verification with AI will soon become as practical as standard testing, and [Theorem's roadmap](https://theorem.dev/blog/verified-software-stack/) already targets critical infrastructure like glibc, OpenSSL, and cURL.

Title: Air Purifiers as White Noise Machines

URL Source: https://www.jefftk.com/p/air-purifiers-as-white-noise-machines

Markdown Content:
White noise machines are widely used for sound masking, increasing privacy in offices and helping people sleep. The [classic approach](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/27/style/white-noise-machines.html) is a fan in a box, though in the past ten years people have mostly switched over to electronic ones. But a fan is really a great approach; you just need to put it to better use: have the fan clean the air.

Instead of spinning a fan in free air to make noise, you can have it pull air through a filter. A small purifier sounds a lot like a classic noise machine, is only a bit larger and more expensive, and removes smoke and infectious particles from the air. For example, [here's a $47 purifier](https://www.amazon.com/LEVOIT-Purifiers-Freshener-Core-Mini/dp/B09GTRVJQM/?th=1) with a 6.5" diameter, cleaning [34 cubic feet of air per minute](https://levoit.com/products/core-mini-p-air-purifier) ("CADR") at 45dB. For most circumstances where someone would use a white noise machine, this kind of small purifier is all-around better.

Now, 34 CFM is not very much air cleaning. I usually run an [AirFanta 3Pro](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D9D5L15F) and it cleans ~6x more air for the same amount of noise, or ~12x more air with much more noise (~56dB). On the other hand it's more expensive ($165) and bulkier (12.6" square), and arguably uglier.

Still, even a 34 CFM purifier helps a lot with smoke. If you have a 10ft square room with an 8ft ceiling and a reasonably typical 0.5 air changes per hour through leakage from outdoors, this small purifier will cut particulate levels to 16% of the outdoor level. In AQI terms (not linear) this is like going from AQI 200 to 72 or AQI 100 to 31.

articles.content:
Title: Microsoft Says Its New AI Is More Than Twice as Good at Diagnosing Diseases as Doctors

URL Source: https://gizmodo.com/microsoft-says-its-new-ai-is-more-than-twice-as-good-at-diagnosing-diseases-as-doctors-2000829562

Published Time: 2026-10-22T20:40:46+00:00

Markdown Content:
Microsoft says its medical AI system can diagnose difficult cases more than twice as accurately as practicing doctors.

Dubbed the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), the system “substantially outperformed practicing generalist physicians” in diagnostic accuracy while ordering fewer tests and procedures, according to a newly published paper.

The Microsoft study, titled “Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models,” was first posted online last year on arXiv as a non-peer-reviewed preprint. On Thursday, the findings were finally [published in the peer-reviewed journal](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aeh7930)_[Science](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aeh7930)_.

That’s a major step toward validating the findings, but any real-world deployment would still require clinical testing, Microsoft’s AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1016690/suleyman-microsoft-diagnostic-orchestrator-science-medical-superintelligence). Microsoft already has plans for that: the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, told the publication that testing will begin at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts, within the next couple of months.

In tests involving complex medical cases published in The New England Journal of Medicine, DxO achieved 83.2% diagnostic accuracy, compared with 36.1% for generalist physicians who had access to reference materials. When physicians were denied those resources, their accuracy dropped to roughly 22%, making DxO nearly four times as accurate. In a separate test involving emergency department admissions, Microsoft’s AI again outperformed generalist physicians, though by a narrower margin of 80.3% to 46.8%. The system achieved its strongest results using OpenAI’s GPT-5, with additional testing showing improvements using GPT-5.5.

“It also manages to do this at half or even one third of the cost, getting to the right diagnosis with fewer tests and procedures,” Microsoft said in a [blog post](https://microsoft.ai/news/building-medical-superintelligence/) Thursday. Those savings, however, are based on estimated costs in simulated cases rather than actual medical expenses. The researchers admitted that they “would expect the performance gap to narrow” if DxO were compared with expert specialists rather than generalists.

Notably, DxO works sequentially, meaning patients don’t simply present the system with a comprehensive list of symptoms, medical history, and test results. Instead, it starts with a chief complaint and must determine which follow-up questions to ask and tests to order before arriving at a diagnosis. That’s much closer to how doctors actually diagnose patients. The researchers say benchmarks have previously failed to evaluate LLMs’ diagnostic capabilities sequentially and propose a new benchmark called the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark, or SDBench.

DxO “simulates a panel of physicians,” the paper explains, “continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests.” The system assigns different roles to AI agents that propose diagnoses, select tests, challenge assumptions, and weigh costs. Researchers suggest this approach can help counter some of the cognitive biases that affect individual physicians, such as anchoring on an initial diagnosis or overlooking alternative explanations.

Similar claims have been made about other companies’ AI tools. Earlier this year, researchers from Harvard University and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center found that [OpenAI’s o1-preview reasoning model](https://gizmodo.com/ai-just-beat-doctors-at-diagnosing-er-patients-dont-get-all-excited-2000752676) outperformed physicians in diagnosing emergency room patients during triage.

In all these cases, medical experts emphasize that superior performance on diagnostic tests doesn’t mean AI systems can or should replace human doctors. Instead, the tools are being positioned as assistants to medical professionals. Even if DxO performs well in clinical trials, widespread adoption would raise difficult legal questions about accountability when an AI-assisted diagnosis goes wrong. And for what it’s worth, [a 2025 study](https://gizmodo.com/doctors-were-worse-at-spotting-cancer-after-leaning-on-ai-study-finds-2000642527) found that doctors who relied on AI to identify potential cancer risks during colonoscopies performed worse than before once the technology was taken away.

articles.content:
Title: A whirlwind tour of systemd-nspawn containers

URL Source: https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/22/whirlwind-tour-of-systemd-nspawn-containers/

Published Time: 2025-03-22T03:43:38-04:00

Markdown Content:
In the [last yearly update](https://quantum5.ca/2024/12/31/2024-year-in-review/), I talked about isolating my self-hosted LLMs running in [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) as well as [Open WebUI](https://openwebui.com/) in `systemd-nspawn` containers and promised a blog post about it. However, while writing that blog post, a footnote on why I am using it instead of Docker accidentally turned into a [full blog post on its own](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/18/docker-considered-harmful/). Here’s the actual post on `systemd-nspawn`.

Fundamentally, `systemd-nspawn` is a lightweight Linux namespaces-based container technology, not dissimilar to [Docker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Docker_(software)). The difference is mostly in image management—instead of describing how to build images with `Dockerfile`s and distributing prebuilt, read-only images containing ready-to-run software, `systemd-nspawn` is typically used with a writable root filesystem, functioning more similarly to a virtual machine. For those of you who remember using [`chroot`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chroot) to run software on a different Linux distro, it can also be described as `chroot` on steroids.

I find `systemd-nspawn` especially useful in the following scenarios:

1.   When you want to run some software with some degree of isolation on a VPS, where you can’t create a full virtual machine due to nested virtualization not being available[1](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/22/whirlwind-tour-of-systemd-nspawn-containers/#fn:nested);
2.   When you need to share access to hardware, such as a GPU (which is why I run LLMs in `systemd-nspawn`);
3.   When you don’t want the overhead of virtualization;
4.   When you want to directly access some files on the host system without resorting to `virtiofs`; and
5.   When you would normally use Docker but can’t or don’t want to. For reasons, please see the [footnote-turned-blog post](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/18/docker-considered-harmful/).

In this post, I’ll describe the process of setting up `systemd-nspawn` containers and how to use them in some common scenarios.

**Update (2025-05-19)**: added [safer Alpine container creation instructions](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/22/whirlwind-tour-of-systemd-nspawn-containers/#installing-alpine-linux-with-alpine-nspawn-install) and [some more guidance](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/22/whirlwind-tour-of-systemd-nspawn-containers/#alpine-linux-notes) on setting up Alpine Linux containers.

## Start with a `chroot`

`systemd-nspawn`, like all containers, requires a separate rootfs in a directory. Since it doesn’t come with an image manager to build images for you, you’ll need to use the traditional Unix approach of creating a `chroot`. It is, after all, `chroot` on steroids.

For `systemd-nspawn`, the typical convention is to put these rootfses under `/var/lib/machines/[hostname]`, where the hostname is that of the container. For this exercise, I’ll just use the name of the OS as the hostname.

Each Linux distro has its own way of creating a new rootfs, so we’ll go through some of the more common ones. I am testing all this on Debian, but there’s no reason why you wouldn’t be able to do any of this on another distro by substituting the equivalent packages. Still, I’ll probably go deeper into Debian because I am more familiar with it.

### `debootstrap` on the Debian family

[`debootstrap`](https://wiki.debian.org/Debootstrap) has featured on this blog many times, mostly when doing crazy things like [installing Debian by hand from rescue systems](https://quantum5.ca/2024/08/12/installing-debian-proxmox-by-hand-from-rescue-environment/). For Debian-based distros like Ubuntu or Debian itself, this is the tool to use to create a rootfs.

On a Debian-based OS, install it with `sudo apt install debootstrap`. It may also be packaged on other distros, or you can just download it from Debian’s repositories:

Either way you installed `debootstrap`, let’s create the rootfs in `/var/lib/machines/debian`:

Copy

```
$ sudo debootstrap --include=systemd,dbus,locales,bash-completion,curl bookworm /var/lib/machines/debian
I: Target architecture can be executed
I: Retrieving InRelease
...
I: Base system installed successfully.
```

Here, we’ve installed `bookworm`, but feel free to substitute this for the latest Debian release. To avoid silly issues, I ensured that `systemd` and `dbus` are installed, along with `locales` to avoid weird warnings in `apt`, `bash-completion` so I don’t hate my life when typing in commands by hand, and `curl` so you can download stuff later. Some of these require a bit of additional configuration later, which we’ll do once we boot into the container.

### Installing RHEL-derivatives with `dnf`

First, install `dnf` and `rpm` if you are on another distro, e.g. on Debian:

Copy

```
$ sudo apt install dnf rpm
...
Setting up dnf (4.14.0-3+deb12u1) ...
Setting up rpm (4.18.0+dfsg-1+deb12u1) ...
...
$ sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/rpm
$ sudo rpm --initdb
```

Then, we make a Fedora 41 chroot as an example:

Copy

```
$ sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/machines/fedora/etc/dnf
$ sudo tee /var/lib/machines/fedora/etc/dnf/dnf.conf > /dev/null
[fedora]
name=Fedora $releasever - $basearch
metalink=https://mirrors.fedoraproject.org/metalink?repo=fedora-$releasever&arch=$basearch
gpgkey=https://getfedora.org/static/fedora.gpg

[updates]
name=Fedora $releasever - $basearch - Updates
metalink=https://mirrors.fedoraproject.org/metalink?repo=updates-released-f$releasever&arch=$basearch
gpgkey=https://getfedora.org/static/fedora.gpg
$ sudo dnf --releasever=41 --best --setopt=install_weak_deps=False --repo=fedora --repo=updates --installroot=/var/lib/machines/fedora install dnf fedora-release glibc glibc-langpack-en iproute iputils less ncurses passwd systemd systemd-networkd systemd-resolved util-linux vim-default-editor
...
Transaction Summary
================================================================================
Install  137 Packages

Total download size: 62 M
Installed size: 206 M
Is this ok [y/N]: y
...
Complete!
```

### Installing Alpine Linux with `alpine-nspawn-install`

Alpine Linux is commonly used in Docker images due to its lightweight size, so I thought I might as well try creating an Alpine Linux chroot. The usual tool for this sort of thing is [`alpine-chroot-install`](https://github.com/alpinelinux/alpine-chroot-install), but its default behaviour is **horrifying** for our use case. For example:

1.   If the current directory is inside `/home`, it binds it into the chroot it configures for “compatibility reasons,” without any warning. I almost **accidentally deleted my entire home directory** when running `rm -rf` on the chroot…
2.   It mounts `/dev`, `/proc`, and `/sys` into the chroot as well. In the case of `/dev`, any subsequent attempt to `chown` the container to take advantage of UID isolation would `chown` all the devices on the host system as well, leading to a disaster that fortunately could be fixed by rebooting.

It is possible to run a crazy `umount` command afterward to clean up after `alpine-chroot-install`, such as:

Copy

```
mount | grep /var/lib/machines/alpine | cut -d' ' -f3 | sort -r | while read -r path; do sudo umount "$path"; done
```

However, I deem this a ticking time-bomb waiting to explode in someone’s face, so instead, I **forked the script** and created [`alpine-nspawn-install`](https://github.com/quantum5/alpine-nspawn-install). My version removes all the crazy “features” of `alpine-chroot-install` that don’t make sense for `systemd-nspawn`, e.g. the mounting, chroot helper scripts, `qemu` support, etc.[2](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/22/whirlwind-tour-of-systemd-nspawn-containers/#fn:aci), while installing a more sane list of packages by default. You can use it like this:

Now let’s see if Alpine lives up to its reputation:

Copy

```
$ sudo du -sh /var/lib/machines/debian
338M	/var/lib/machines/debian
$ sudo du -sh /var/lib/machines/fedora
507M	/var/lib/machines/fedora
$ sudo du -sh /var/lib/machines/alpine
16M	/var/lib/machines/alpine
```

Well, that’s certainly impressive… Alpine is an order of magnitude smaller than the other two, while Fedora is quite bloated with the list of packages I have installed. I am not a Fedora user and copied the package list from the [Arch Linux wiki guide on `systemd-nspawn`](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Systemd-nspawn), so I am not sure if it’s because I’ve installed bloat, but they all seem pretty necessary… It’s certainly bigger than what `dnf` claimed to be, so I took a look, and `dnf` created 260 MiB of stuff under `/var/cache/dnf`.

Also to be fair to Debian, I did install a bunch of “bloat” like locales for a more pleasant experience. Removing the “bloat” results in 305 MiB, which is slightly smaller.

## Initial boot with `systemd-nspawn`

First, install `systemd-nspawn` with `sudo apt install systemd-container` or your distro’s equivalent.

Then, you can get a root shell in a container by running the following command:

Copy

```
$ sudo systemd-nspawn -D /var/lib/machines/[name] -M [name] --private-users=pick --private-users-ownership=chown
```

And here is what each argument does:

*   `-D` (`--directory`) specifies the directory of the rootfs;
*   `-M` (`--machine`) specifies the machine name, which is also set as the hostname inside the container;
*   `--private-users=pick` enables UID and GID namespaces by picking a range of 65536 UIDs and GIDs from an unused block on the host system starting from a multiple of 65536 in the range of 524288 and 1878982656[3](https://quantum5.ca/2025/03/22/whirlwind-tour-of-systemd-nspawn-containers/#fn:uid-bit). Alternative options include `yes`, which selects the range starting from the owning UID and GID of the rootfs (must be a multiple of 65536); `no`, which disables UID namespacing; an integer, which serves as starting UID for a block of 65536; or a string of the format `a:b`, where `a` is the starting UID and the number of UIDs to assign to the container; and finally
*   `--private-users-ownership=chown` changes the ownership of the rootfs to that of the UID and GID chosen so that on future boots, `--private-users=yes` will keep using the same UIDs and GIDs.

Let’s boot Debian as an example:

Copy

```
$ sudo systemd-nspawn -D /var/lib/machines/debian -M debian --private-users=pick --private-users-ownership=chown
Spawning container debian on /var/lib/machines/debian.
Press ^] three times within 1s to kill container.
Selected user namespace base 1766326272 and range 65536.
root@debian:~#
```

And we are in the newly created Debian container. Note that this is **just** a root shell and isn’t a proper way to deploy the container long term. There is no `init` process even.

### Debian-specific setup tips

If you are going to be using a root shell for a significant amount of time and want autocomplete to avoid typing entire commands:

Copy

```
root@debian:~# cp /etc/skel/.bashrc .
root@debian:~# . ~/.bashrc
```

If you are just using the container to run a single application, it can get really tedious to manage your own users and then sudo, so I just opt to do the management as root and having a functioning `.bashrc` works wonders. This is technically not best practice, but I basically never run commands in single application containers that don’t require `root` anyway, so it makes no real difference.

`debootstrap` also copied the host’s hostname into `/etc/hostname`. Let’s fix that:

Copy

```
root@debian:~# hostname > /etc/hostname
```

### Getting back into the container

If you exited the root shell for some reason, you can go back by doing:

Copy

```
$ sudo systemd-nspawn -D /var/lib/machines/debian -M debian --private-users=yes
Spawning container debian on /var/lib/machines/debian.
Press ^] three times w
